rashi:a1.1: Mishna. Communal offerings: They are all males, since most of them are burnt offerings, and a burnt offering is a male. And the community brings no peace offerings except the lambs of Shavuot [Atzeret], which are males. And their sin offerings are goats, as is written with regard to all of them: “And one goat for a sin offering.”
rashi:a2.1: Offerings of an individual: one is obligated to bring their compensation: That is, some of them, among those that have a fixed time, even if their time has passed one is obligated to sacrifice them, for example the burnt offering of a woman after childbirth, and the offerings of a leper: if his eighth day has passed, he can sacrifice it after its time. But communal offerings that have a set time, if their time has passed, their offering is void, as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a2.2: Once the offering is sacrificed: That if the offering was sacrificed at its time and the libations were not sacrificed with it, one is obligated to sacrifice them, even ten days from now, as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a4.1: The High Priest’s griddle-cake offerings: They override Shabbat and impurity, as it is written of them: “A meal offering perpetually [tamid]” [Leviticus 6:13]; it is like the meal offering of the daily offerings [temidin], [as stated] at the end of [the chapter] HaTekhelet in Menaḥot (50b).
rashi:a4.2: The bull of Yom Kippur: The bull of Aaron [i.e., of the High Priest].
rashi:a4.3: Rather, whose time is fixed: That is, the reason depends only on the fixing of the time. Those whose time is fixed, which have no compensation if the time has passed, override Shabbat and impurity, even those of an individual; and all those that have no fixed time do not override Shabbat and impurity, even communal ones, for example the bull for an unwitting communal sin [he’elem davar shel tzibbur] and the goats for idol worship.
rashi:a7.1: Gemara. The primary offering: The first consecrated animal.
rashi:a8.1: You can even say it is the Rabbis: Who do not hold that the offspring renders a substitute.
rashi:a9.1: Both males and females: This implies that every offering that an individual is obligated to bring [may come] either as a male or as a female.
rashi:a10.1: There is the bird burnt offering: This is an answer.
rashi:a12.1: A guilt offering: It is a male, since “a lamb” or “a ram” is written with regard to it, and not a ewe.
rashi:a12.2: What are they? Peace offerings: But communal peace offerings are males, as it is written of them: “And two male lambs in their first year as a sacrifice of peace offerings” (Leviticus 23:19). The communal peace offerings are the lambs of Shavuot [Atzeret].
rashi:a13.1: From where are these matters derived: That communal offerings have no compensation.
rashi:a14.1: Each day on its own day: It speaks of the additional offerings of the Festivals, in the section “An ox or a sheep” [Leviticus 22:27 and on], as it is written: “These are the appointed seasons of the Lord, holy convocations, etc., to bring an offering made by fire.” And which offering made by fire does one sacrifice on a Festival beyond other days? You must say: the additional offerings.
rashi:a14.2: That the entire day is fit for the additional offerings: Provided that the additional offerings precede the afternoon daily offering, as it says (Yoma 33a): “Upon it complete all the offerings” [i.e., the afternoon daily offering concludes the day’s service].
rashi:a15.1: Their meal offerings and their libations, even at night and even on the morrow: If the offering was sacrificed at its time, [the libations may be brought] even ten days from now, and indefinitely. And it is speaking of a case where they were not available to him [at the time].
rashi:a16.1: Beside the Shabbatot of the Lord: For so it is written: “A sacrifice and libations, each day on its own day; beside the Shabbatot of the Lord.” And because we expound juxtaposed verses: “each day on its own day,” sacrifice libations, besides those of the Shabbatot; that is, if a Festival falls after Shabbat, sacrifice its libations with its offerings, and sacrifice the libations that you forgot yesterday and did not sacrifice.
rashi:a17.1: On the day, yes; at night, no: For “each day on its own day” is written, and juxtaposed to it is “beside the Shabbatot of the Lord.” That is, sacrifice the libations of Shabbat today, on the Festival, but not at night.
rashi:a17.2: And if it had written “their meal offerings and their libations,” I would say: [It comes] to teach you that you may sacrifice the libations of the day on the night that follows, but not on the following day.
rashi:a18.1: And what is different: That is, and if you would say: Why should it be different, that one would say at night, yes, by day, no? The verse is written without qualification.
rashi:a18.2: Because with regard to sacrificial animals the night follows the day: that has passed, as it is written: “On the day of his offering it shall be eaten; you shall not leave any of it until the morning” (Leviticus 7:15). Evidently it calls the whole night “the day of his offering.” Therefore it might enter your mind that at night it may be sacrificed, since the libations are [still considered] of the day that passed, but not on the following day.
rashi:a19.1: I have only, etc.: It is in Torat Kohanim [the Sifra], and refers to the verse that is written: “It is that which goes up on its firewood upon the altar all night,” that one places them from sunset and they are consumed all night.
rashi:a19.2: I have only items that are normally sacrificed at night, for example: The limbs of a burnt offering and the fats, which were included above for this, that one places them from sunset, that is, after the setting of the sun one places them on the arrangement of wood.
rashi:a20.1: Items that are normally sacrificed in the day: Which are not sacrificed at night at all, since with regard to all the offerings it is written: “On the day that he commanded” [Leviticus 7:38], which implies by day and not at night. But limbs and fats are what is included here, at night, by this verse: that one sacrifices them from sunset and burns them on the arrangement of wood, and they are consumed by themselves. For if not so, what would “it is the burnt offering” exclude?
rashi:a20.2: And he asks: After sunset? But you said it is normally sacrificed in the day!
rashi:a20.3: Rather, with sunset: Before the sun sets.
rashi:a21.1: To consecrate: At night, if they were placed in a service vessel they are consecrated, so they can no longer go out to non-sacred status; but as for being sacrificed, they are not sacrificed until the day.
rashi:a22.1: If they are consecrated: at night, they are also sacrificed [at night].
rashi:a22.2: Delete the libations from here: Do not count them with the items that are normally sacrificed in the day.
rashi:a23.1: With the offering: That are brought with the offering, and the slaughter of the offering consecrated them, so that they are like the offering itself, and they are sacrificed only by day.
rashi:a24.1: Rav Dimi said: If I would find someone who writes a letter: If I would find a person, I would write my letter and send it to Rav Yosef in Babylonia.
tosafot:a22.1: And any that is sacrificed at night: Rashi explained at the end of [the chapter] Shetei HaLeḥem (Menaḥot 100a): for example, oil for the Candelabrum. But this does not seem right, for what sanctity applies to it? It has no sanctity of a vessel. Therefore it seems one should say that we find nothing sacrificed at night except the meal offering that accompanies libations. And because of this it is understandable that [the Gemara] does not answer here: Perhaps it is not consecrated so as to be sacrificed, but it is consecrated so as to become disqualified; for so it concludes there, at the end of the chapter Shetei HaLeḥem, relying on what is taught: “And any that is sacrificed at night,” since we find nothing sacrificed at night except the meal offering of libations alone. And by the same token [the Gemara] could have raised the difficulty from it here explicitly, from the fact that it teaches: “And any that is sacrificed at night,” and we find this only with the meal offering of libations; but it prefers to raise the difficulty even according to what was initially assumed there in the chapter Shetei HaLeḥem.
gershom:a1.1: But there is the offspring of an individual’s offering, and it does not render a substitute: As it says in the previous chapter: “It” [Leviticus 27:10: “then it and its substitute shall be sacred”], and not the offspring.
gershom:a2.1: In accordance with whose opinion is the mishna, which teaches that offerings of an individual render a substitute, even the offspring of an individual’s offering? It is Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:a3.1: But there is the substitute of an individual’s offering, and it does not render another substitute: As it says above: “And not the substitute of its substitute.” When it teaches that offerings of an individual render a substitute, it teaches it of the primary offering itself, and not of a substitute nor of offspring.
gershom:a4.1: And now that you have arrived at this, you can even say the mishna is the Rabbis. And as for the difficulty, “But there is the offspring of an individual’s offering and it does not render a substitute”: when the mishna teaches, it teaches of the primary offering of an individual, that it renders a substitute.
gershom:a5.1: But there is the bird burnt offering: Which comes even as a female; and this is the answer.
gershom:a6.1: But there is the goat sin offering: of a king, which is an individual’s, and it is a male; and this too is an answer.
gershom:a7.1: But there is the guilt offering: An individual’s offering that comes as a male and not as a female.
gershom:a8.1: From where are these matters derived: That one is not obligated to bring compensation for a communal offering.
gershom:a9.1: As the Sages taught: “These are the appointed seasons of the Lord, holy convocations, to bring an offering made by fire to the Lord, a burnt offering, and a meal offering, a sacrifice, and libations, each day on its own day.” “Each day” teaches that the entire day is fit for the additional offerings; that is, “a burnt offering” means the additional offerings.
gershom:a10.1: “On its own day” teaches that if the day has passed and he did not bring them, he is not obligated to bring their compensation, since “on its own day” implies specifically on its own day. Thus if its day has passed, its offering is void and he is not obligated to bring their compensation.
gershom:a11.1: One might have thought he is not obligated to bring compensation for their libations even once the offering has been sacrificed; the verse states in the section of Pinḥas: “And their meal offerings and their libations,” including even at night and even on the morrow, since he is obligated to bring their compensation. Reish Lakish says [it is derived from here] that he is obligated to bring compensation [once the offering has been sacrificed]: from the fact that “beside the Shabbatot of the Lord” is juxtaposed to it. This implies that if a Festival fell after Shabbat, [and they did not sacrifice the libations of the additional offerings of Shabbat on Shabbat,] they bring them now, on the Festival, as it is written: “A sacrifice and libations, each day on its own day; beside the Shabbatot of the Lord.” That is, those of the Festival are sacrificed, and these of yesterday, of Shabbat, are “beside the Shabbatot of the Lord.” Evidently “and their libations” [applies] even on the morrow.
gershom:a12.1: And if you would say, what is different, [that it is at night] that they are sacrificed and not afterward? Because with regard to sacrificial animals the night follows the day, as it is written: “And from the eighth day and onward it shall be accepted” [Leviticus 22:27]; [that is, on the night of the eighth] it is forbidden to slaughter it, since that night completes the seven days [and the animal is still premature]. With regard to a premature animal, then, the night follows the day in sacrificial matters. [Therefore it wrote again “beside the Shabbatot of the Lord” with “on its own day,” to say that on the morrow one brings yesterday’s libations: on the Festival one sacrifices the libations of Shabbat. “After sunset” means once the sun has set.]
gershom:a13.1: Until sunset [ad bo hashemesh; the Gemara reads “with sunset”]: That is, close to, before the sun sets.
gershom:a14.1: “This is the law of the burnt offering” included: all that go up [on the altar].
gershom:a15.1: Here to consecrate, there to sacrifice: To consecrate, one consecrates libations even at night; but to sacrifice, one sacrifices only by day. Rava said: And if they are consecrated at night, they are also sacrificed [at night], as it is taught: This is the principle, etc.
gershom:a16.1: Rather, delete from that baraita of “I have only” the meal offering of libations, because it is also sacrificed at night.
gershom:a17.1: When Rav Dimi ascended, etc.: He said: If I find someone who is going there, I will write a letter and send it to him, that he should not delete the meal offering of libations from the baraita.
gershom:a18.1: Rabbi Meir said: But aren’t the griddle-cake offerings, etc. Rather, whose time is fixed: That is, Rabbi Meir holds there is no difference between them: any offering whose time is fixed, whether of an individual or of the community, overrides Shabbat and impurity.
rashi:b1.1: He will not delete the libations: from that baraita above, and he can answer:
rashi:b1.2: Here: That which teaches libations together with items that are normally sacrificed by day refers to libations that come with the offering.
rashi:b1.3: By themselves: Which were not consecrated by the slaughter of the offering; one can sacrifice them at night.
rashi:b2.1: Like those who burn the Torah: For they are not rescued from a fire on Shabbat. Another explanation: Because it is forbidden to keep them written, since it is the Oral Torah.
rashi:b2.2: And one who learns from them: From the books.
rashi:b5.1: New [ḥadta]: A new matter, in that they did not know how to resolve the baraitot.
rashi:b5.2: [Another version:] Ḥadtei: To innovate something, such as this one, which is new.
rashi:b5.3: Read from a scroll of aggada: So that they would not be forgotten.
rashi:b5.4: It is time to work for the Lord: When one does something for the sake of sanctifying God’s name, it is fitting to make void Your Torah; and it is better that it be uprooted, etc.
rashi:b6.1: Now that you have said, etc.: One can consecrate them and sacrifice them in one night. Another version: we read [here]: “Dawn disqualifies them, like limbs”; that is, as for what we said, that if libations happened to be available at night one consecrates them at night [and sacrifices them, dawn disqualifies them].
rashi:b8.1: Like limbs: of the daily offering, in tractate Zevaḥim (87a). And this is the main version, the emendation of the Master.
rashi:b9.1: Obligatory offerings that come on account of the pilgrimage Festival, on the Festival: For example, the burnt offering of appearance, the Festival peace offering, and the additional offerings.
rashi:b13.2: To include the peace offering of a nazirite: For if voluntary peace offerings [were meant], “your voluntary offerings” was already said; and if [it is written only] for the juxtaposition, let it write [simply] “and to the peace offerings.”
rashi:b14.1: Peace offerings of the Paschal offering: The Festival peace offering of the fourteenth [of Nisan]. When the group registered for the Paschal offering was large and it did not suffice for them, they would bring peace offerings with it. And if one separated them for this purpose and they did not sacrifice them, they sacrifice them on the intermediate days of the Festival. For the nazirite’s peace offerings do not need an inclusion, since they are derived from “your vows and your voluntary offerings”: naziriteship comes upon him through a vow, and it is called vowed and contributed. But the peace offerings of the Paschal offering are obligatory, as is explained in Pesaḥim, in the chapter Ve’elu Devarim (71a).
rashi:b16.1: And the nazirite offerings are sacrificed on a private altar: Evidently it is considered vowed and contributed, for otherwise it would not be sacrificed on a private altar.
rashi:b16.2: Delete the nazirite offerings from here: For even though naziriteship comes upon him through a vow, the offerings are not called vowed and contributed, since he vowed only [to abstain] from wine, and the offering is imposed on him as an obligation of itself.
rashi:b17.1: Which I have vowed to the Lord, in Hebron: This implies: In Hebron I will go and pay my vow there. And that vow was a vow of naziriteship, for Absalom was a permanent nazirite, and every thirty days he would shave and bring an offering. And since he went to sacrifice the offerings of his naziriteship in Hebron, which is a private altar, learn from it that it is vowed and contributed.
rashi:b18.1: It refers to his principal vow: This “in Hebron” [refers to the vow], and this is what he is saying: Let me go to the great altar in Gibeon, for there is the altar that Moses made, and pay my vow that I vowed in Hebron; but not that he would bring the offering in Hebron.
rashi:b18.2: But wasn’t it in Geshur, etc.: As it is written: “For your servant vowed a vow while I dwelled at Geshur,” etc.
rashi:b19.1: To bring sheep: And then to sacrifice them on the great altar. And this is what he is saying: I will pay my vow, that is, I will complete my naziriteship and shave, and from Hebron I will bring the sheep. And this is why he asks: It should have said “from Hebron.”
rashi:b19.2: In Hebron: there are fat sheep, [as stated] in tractate Menaḥot (87a).
rashi:b21.1: Rather, actually to sacrifice: For naziriteship [offerings may be sacrificed] on a private altar.
rashi:b21.2: Gibeon should pose a difficulty for you: For there was the altar that Moses made.
tosafot:b3.1: Words that are written you may not recite orally: And if you will say: How do we recite psalms by heart? One can say that one need be particular only about what is written in the Pentateuch. However, it is difficult: How do we recite “And He saved” [the Song of the Sea] and the Shema [by heart]? One can say that one need be particular only about something with which one fulfills the obligation of others.
tosafot:b16.1: And we learned: The meal offerings and the nazirite offerings are sacrificed on a private altar; this is the statement of Rabbi Meir: [The Gemara] could have answered that it is a dispute of tanna’im, for in the last chapter of Zevaḥim (117a) the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Meir, and it concludes there that the difference between them is meal offerings and nazirite offerings.
tosafot:b16.2: Delete the nazirite offerings from here: And by the same token one must likewise delete it from that [passage] in the last chapter of Zevaḥim (117b), which says: The difference between them is meal offerings and nazirite offerings.
tosafot:b21.1: In brief: Since private altars were permitted, he could sacrifice wherever he wished. (1) According to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Meir and hold that naziriteship is not vowed and contributed, one must say that Absalom went only to bring sheep from Hebron and sacrifice them in Gibeon. (2) But according to Rashi’s explanation in the last chapter of Zevaḥim, that Rabbi Meir’s disputants hold like the later Rabbis there, who say that at both the great and the small altars an individual sacrificed only burnt offerings and peace offerings, it is difficult: How could Absalom say “Let me go and pay my vow,” if for the Rabbis naziriteship is not vowed and contributed and could be sacrificed at neither? One must then divide the tanna’im: Rabbi Meir’s disputants do not hold like the later Rabbis but like Rabbi Yehuda, who says that at the great altar even obligatory offerings were sacrificed; while Rabbi Meir, who holds naziriteship is vowed and contributed, can hold like the later Rabbis of Zevaḥim. Yet the plain flow of the passage there implies as Rashi explained. (3) It is also difficult according to Rabbi Shimon, who says there (Zevaḥim) that even the community sacrificed [at Nov and Gibeon] only Paschal offerings and obligatory offerings with a fixed time; and it says in Pesaḥim (38b), “This is to say that the loaves of a thanks offering and the wafers of a nazirite were eaten in Nov and Gibeon,” which Rashi there explains is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon. If so, how could Absalom say “Let me go and pay my vow,” since he could not sacrifice it? Their teacher, HaRaMaR, answered that Rabbi Shimon follows his own view in tractate Nazir (46b): if a nazirite shaved on voluntary peace offerings he has fulfilled his obligation, and if he said, “I will shave on one hundred burnt offerings,” he brings one hundred burnt offerings. So Absalom may have vowed voluntary burnt offerings, which everyone agrees are sacrificed at a private altar, and wished to shave on them. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: And it is not difficult: The mishna teaches that once the offering has been sacrificed one is obligated to bring compensation for them, that is, even at night; and the baraita that teaches “and their meal offerings and their libations,” at night, refers to libations that come by themselves: he did not consecrate them with the offering, but consecrated them after the sacrifice of the offering, since a person can sacrifice his offering today and its libations even ten days from now; and of these it says that they are sacrificed even at night. And what the baraita teaches among items normally sacrificed by day, the meal offering of libations, refers to libations that come with the offering.
gershom:b2.1: Those who write halakhot: The midrash of the Mishna, and Talmud and aggadot, [matters of the Oral Law; they are punished] like those who burn the Torah, because the law is that halakhot are oral and one is not permitted to write them. And anyone who learns from them, from writing, has no reward.
gershom:b3.1: Words that are written: The Torah, Prophets and Writings. A new matter is different: That juxtaposition was a new matter, and therefore it is permitted [to write it].
gershom:b4.1: Another version: Because there is [a concern of] forgetting, they write; and why is it permitted?
gershom:b5.1: Better that [one letter of the Torah] be uprooted, [the letter] where it is written “for by the mouth”; and it is better to write, so that the Torah not be forgotten.
gershom:b6.1: Now that you have said that libations that come by themselves, after the sacrifice of the offering, [and on account of] the offering, are sacrificed even at night: If they happened to be available to him, he consecrates them at night in a service vessel and sacrifices them at night, since he is obligated to bring their compensation.
gershom:b7.1: Rav Adda bar Ahava said: The dawn burnt offering [Rabbeinu Gershom reads olat, “burnt offering of,” for alot, “rising of”], i.e., the daily offering, disqualifies them like the limbs. And this refers to the baraita that teaches “and they are consumed throughout the entire night”: if all the limbs of the afternoon daily offering were not consumed by the time they offered up the morning daily offering, it disqualifies the limbs. But arranging the wood for the morning daily offering does not disqualify them; only the sacrifice of [the daily offering] itself, since it is already day and it is not their manner to be sacrificed by day.
gershom:b8.1: [“Beside your vows and your voluntary offerings” teaches about vows and voluntary offerings] that they are sacrificed on the intermediate days of the Festival, which is also “your appointed seasons”; but not on the Festival day itself, for vows and voluntary offerings are not sacrificed on a Festival day.
gershom:b9.1: Consequently, the verse speaks only of the burnt offering of a woman after childbirth and the burnt offering of a leper, which are also sacrificed on the intermediate days of the Festival.
gershom:b10.1: The sinner’s meal offering and the meal offering of jealousy [Rabbeinu Gershom names both; the daf names only the meal offering of a sota]: These too are sacrificed on the intermediate days of the Festival.
gershom:b11.1: So too libations by day: Those that come with the offering.
gershom:b12.1: These are the nazirite’s peace offerings: Which are also sacrificed on the intermediate days of the Festival.
gershom:b13.1: And let the Master say: peace offerings of the Paschal offering, which come as an obligation with the Paschal offering, as it is written: “And you shall sacrifice peace offerings and eat there” [Deuteronomy 27:7].
gershom:b14.1: For if the nazirite’s peace offerings, it is something vowed and contributed: For a person vows to be a nazirite, counts his naziriteship and afterward brings his peace offerings, and it already taught about vows and voluntary offerings that they are sacrificed on the intermediate days. If so, why do I need “and your peace offerings”?
gershom:b15.1: And from where do we derive that a nazirite’s offering is something vowed and contributed? As we learned: This is the principle: Something vowed and contributed is sacrificed on a private altar.
gershom:b16.1: And it is taught: The meal offerings and the nazirite are sacrificed on a private altar. Evidently the nazirite’s peace offerings are something vowed and contributed, since they are sacrificed on a private altar. Rather, Rav Yosef said [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text attributes the deletion to Rav Yosef; the daf leaves it unattributed and the Davidson English gives it to Rav Dimi]: Delete from that baraita “the meal offerings and the nazirite offerings”; do not teach that the nazirite offerings are sacrificed on a private altar, and one cannot say that it is vowed and contributed. And Rav Dimi holds it is a dispute of tanna’im: this is Rabbi Meir, [who holds] they are sacrificed on a private altar, and that is the Rabbis, who disagree with him [and hold] it is not sacrificed on a private altar, since it is not vowed and contributed; and I say in accordance with the Rabbis.
gershom:b17.1: No, it refers to his principal vow, which he vowed in Hebron: to count naziriteship; that is his principal vow.
gershom:b18.1: He was a permanent nazirite, and he would shave [from year to year] in Hebron, and he was there? This is said in astonishment: That is, [as for his vow in general,] what difference does it make where he vowed, and why would he go there on account of that? And furthermore, his vow was in Geshur.
gershom:b19.1: That he went to take sheep from Hebron: As it is taught: Rams from Moab and sheep from Hebron. For if you do not say so, it was a naziriteship outside the Land, since he vowed while dwelling at Geshur in Aram, and it does not count toward his tally, for so we learned in tractate Nazir: “One who vowed a lengthy naziriteship…”
